subject: reading a folder that contains multiple word docs and pdf files

messages.author: dc00a99e2f28f20f
messages.subject: reading a folder that contains multiple word docs and pdf files
parts:
Hello,

Someone at work was trying to search a very large hard drive using
the Microsoft search engine. I thought R would do a better job.

The data is located in a folder called Clinical reports which has two
sub-folders (named central & southern) and then each of these have
sub-folders (2005, 2006, 2007, etc)

e.g "G://FMH/Common/Clinicalreports" . The files contained in these
folders are either in MS-Word format or pdf format.

I want to be able to search for find specified words and identify
which files they are in. Is this possible?

Any assistance is much appreciated,

regards

Bob

messages.author: d95dc06d463d4250
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] reading a folder that contains multiple word  docs and pdf files
parts:
I used to work in text retrieval (what y'all call search engines now).
I'm not convinced that such a specific task is suited to either
Microsoft's offering or to R. Especially since you make no mention of
data volume other than there being a very large drive. How many
documents/year? How many words per document? Is this a one off
requirement or a regular task? Are you only looking to find which
files contain the word (why not a phrase)?

You might to better to look at using Apache's Lucene text retrieval
system or a derivative of it. But without more data on the data
there's nothing else to recommend.

parts:
PowerGREP would do what you want, but it comes at a cost (US$149).

From the publisher's website (http://www.powergrep.com/):

"PowerGREP is a powerful Windows grep tool. Quickly search through large
numbers of files on your PC or network, including text and binary files,
compressed archives, MS Word documents, Excel spreadsheets, PDF files,
OpenOffice files, etc. Find the information you want with powerful text
patterns (regular expressions) specifying the form of what you want,
instead of literal text. Search and replace with one or many regular
expressions to comprehensively maintain web sites, source code, reports,
etc. Extract statistics and knowledge from logs files and large data
sets."

John

Thanks for your replies. I can check the volume of the main drive but
there would be 1000s of files. The datafiles of interest probably
number 500-600 and produce about a 100 per year. For another purpose
we calculated the average length of a sub-set of these files and it
was 14 pages. Typically we are looking for an individual word

(stalker, stalking, harassment, obsession). The individual searches
night be run only a few times, but there will be a number of such
searches that can run over a year.

Feel free to seek further clarification. I work for a public service
agency where there isn't much in the way of resources for such things
so cost is a factor.

regards

Bob

messages.author: d95dc06d463d4250
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Re: reading a folder that contains multiple  word docs and pdf files
parts:
Bob,

In that case and assuming that the only analsysis is the *presence* of
these words, synonms or collocates then I'd go with Lucene. Check out
http://lucene.apache.org/ for details. There are input modules to deal
with both Microsoft Word formats and with PDF. But yo'll have to dig
for them. Keep the Lucene index files around and later searches will
be quicker as it won't have to rescan the old texts. I don't recall
the details but it's something like O(n log(n)) for a Lucene search,
where n is the number of documents to be scanned/searched. (A grep
solution is O(n).)

Of course if you're going to do *any* analysis of the texts then you
will have to look at R and also probabaly the tm text mining package,
The paper in the Journal of Statistical Software at
http://www.jstatsoft.org/v25/i05 describes that package's
capabilities. Supposed to cope with both Word and PDF encoded
documents; my personal use is only with plain text files. You may be
able to manipulate your "large disk of documents" as a repository
within tm, though we might well refer to these repositories as
corpora.

And of course, Lucene, R and the tm package have the benefit of
zero-cost licenses.
